name: Airway & Procedures
sub: RSI, difficult airway, lines, drains, tracheostomy, LP

cards.q: Give typical rapid-sequence induction doses for the common induction agents.
cards.a: Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg, ketamine 1–2 mg/kg, propofol 1–2 mg/kg (reduce or avoid in shock). Reduce the dose in shock, elderly or frail patients, and prepare vasopressors before induction.

cards.q: Give RSI neuromuscular blocker doses and the reversal of rocuronium.
cards.a: Succinylcholine 1–1.5 mg/kg or rocuronium 1.0–1.2 mg/kg. Sugammadex 16 mg/kg reverses rocuronium immediately in a cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate situation.

cards.q: List contraindications to succinylcholine.
cards.a: Hyperkalaemia, burns or crush injury beyond about 24–48 hours, prolonged immobilisation or denervation (stroke, spinal cord injury, neuromuscular disease), history of malignant hyperthermia, plasma cholinesterase deficiency.

cards.q: What does the LEMON assessment evaluate?
cards.a: Difficult laryngoscopy: Look externally, Evaluate 3-3-2 rule, Mallampati, Obstruction, Neck mobility.

cards.q: What does the DAS difficult-airway plan sequence include?
cards.a: Plan A: tracheal intubation; Plan B: supraglottic airway; Plan C: face-mask ventilation and waking; Plan D: front-of-neck access (scalpel-bougie-tube cricothyroidotomy) in cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate.

cards.q: How should you preoxygenate before intubation and prolong safe apnoea time?
cards.a: At least 3 minutes of tidal breathing at high FiO₂ with head-up positioning, or NIV/HFNC in hypoxaemic patients, plus apnoeic oxygenation with nasal cannula at 15 L/min or HFNC during laryngoscopy.

cards.x: The gold-standard confirmation of tracheal tube placement is {{c1::continuous waveform capnography}}; the tip should sit about {{c2::3–5 cm}} above the carina on chest X-ray.

cards.q: What is the typical ETT depth at the teeth for adults?
cards.a: About 21 cm for women and 23 cm for men; also approximately three times the tube's internal diameter.

cards.q: How do you minimise haemodynamic collapse during intubation of a shocked patient?
cards.a: Resuscitate before you intubate: give fluids or blood if indicated, start vasopressors, reduce induction dose (ketamine or etomidate), use a push-dose pressor, and preoxygenate well to avoid hypoxic arrest.

cards.q: Which sites are recommended for central venous catheters and what technique?
cards.a: Ultrasound-guided right internal jugular is commonly first choice; subclavian carries lower infection but higher pneumothorax risk; femoral carries higher infection and thrombosis risk. Use Seldinger technique, full barrier precautions and chlorhexidine skin preparation.

cards.q: Name the CLABSI prevention bundle elements.
cards.a: Hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions, chlorhexidine skin preparation, optimal insertion site (avoid femoral), daily review of the need for the line, and prompt removal of unnecessary catheters.

cards.q: What is the 'safe triangle' for chest-drain insertion?
cards.a: Bounded by the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, the lateral border of pectoralis major and a line above the nipple (fifth intercostal space), apex below the axilla. Insert just above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

cards.q: How do you position and confirm a lumbar puncture?
cards.a: Lateral decubitus with spine flexed, needle at L3–L4 or L4–L5 (the iliac crest line is about L4). Contraindicated with raised ICP from mass effect, coagulopathy or local infection; check imaging when there are focal signs or reduced consciousness.

cards.q: What is the role and timing of tracheostomy in ventilated patients?
cards.a: Considered when prolonged ventilation is expected (often after 7–14 days). Early (<10 days) tracheostomy did not change mortality in TracMan, but may reduce sedation and improve comfort.

cards.q: What are the signs of a cannulation-site pneumothorax after a central line?
cards.a: New dyspnoea, chest pain, reduced breath sounds, falling SpO₂ or rising airway pressure in ventilated patients, absent lung sliding on ultrasound; confirm with ultrasound or chest X-ray.

cards.q: How do you confirm central venous catheter placement quickly at the bedside?
cards.a: Ultrasound shows a rapid atrial swirl after a saline flush ('bubble test') in the right atrium; exclude pneumothorax by looking for lung sliding; chest X-ray confirms tip position at the cavo-atrial junction.

cards.q: What is the usual first defibrillation energy for a biphasic defibrillator?
cards.a: 120–200 J (manufacturer-specific); use the maximum available if unknown, and escalate or keep the same for subsequent shocks.

cards.q: A tube is placed and the capnography trace is flat after intubation. What should you assume?
o: Oesophageal intubation until proven otherwise; remove the tube and re-oxygenate
The patient is in cardiac arrest only
The monitor is faulty and you can proceed
cards.e: A flat trace may also mean cardiac arrest, disconnection or complete obstruction, but you must confirm tube position directly. When in doubt, take it out.

cards.q: After two failed intubation attempts, SpO₂ is 82% and falling, with difficult mask ventilation. What is the next step?
o: Insert a second-generation supraglottic airway and call for help
Make a third attempt with the same blade
Wake the patient and abandon oxygenation
cards.e: Limit attempts, oxygenate between them, and move to Plan B. If still unable to oxygenate, proceed to front-of-neck access.

cards.q: How do you prepare for a bedside percutaneous tracheostomy?
cards.a: Check coagulation and platelets, stop feeds, use bronchoscopic or ultrasound guidance, adjust FiO₂ to 1.0, paralyse and sedate, and have a plan for a lost airway (surgical set, difficult airway trolley).

cards.q: What is the role of videolaryngoscopy in the ICU?
cards.a: It improves first-pass success and glottic view, especially in difficult airways, and reduces complications; it is recommended as first-line when available for critically ill intubations.
